Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 21, 2023, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published its operational statistics for the month of September 2023. The report indicated a significant increase in migrant encounters at the southwest border, with a total of 269,735 encounters recorded for the month. In response to the high rates of encounters, CBP stated it had surged resources and personnel. The agency also highlighted its ongoing engagement with domestic and foreign partners to address what it described as historic hemispheric migration. A key development noted in the announcement was the resumption of direct removal flights of Venezuelan nationals to their home country. <2> On October 20, 2023, the White House announced a national security supplemental funding request of nearly $106 billion. [1, 3, 5] The proposal earmarked $13.6 billion for border security, which included funding to hire an additional 1,300 Border Patrol agents, 1,600 asylum officers and associated support staff, and to create 375 more immigration judge teams. [1, 5, 7] The comprehensive package was designed to provide aid to Ukraine and Israel, invest in the domestic defense industry, and manage migration at the U.S.-Mexico border by enhancing measures against drug trafficking and increasing personnel for processing asylum cases. [3, 4, 5] <3> The Biden administration resumed direct deportation flights to Venezuela on October 18, 2023, with the first charter flight carrying approximately 130 migrants from Harlingen, Texas, to Caracas. [4, 6, 7] This action followed the administration's announcement on October 5, 2023, that it would restart repatriations to the South American country, a policy that had been stalled for years due to strained diplomatic relations. [3, 8, 9] The flight, operated by ICE contractor iAero Airways, made a stop in Miami before arriving in Venezuela. [4, 11] U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials stated that the passengers included recent arrivals and that multiple similar flights were planned for the following weeks. [4, 6] The resumption of deportations was part of a broader administration strategy to create consequences for unlawful border crossings while expanding legal pathways for migration. [4, 10] <4> In early October 2023, Senate Republicans, led by Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, formally linked their support for any additional aid to Ukraine with the passage of significant security enhancements at the U.S. southern border. This strategic move prompted the formation of a bipartisan group of senators, with the endorsement of both party leaders, to begin negotiations on a comprehensive bill. The goal was to craft legislation that could garner enough bipartisan support to overcome opposition from both progressive and conservative factions and address both pressing issues simultaneously. <5> On September 25, 2023, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) announced it was exempting the $85 biometric services fee for all Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status. This policy change, which made a previous temporary suspension permanent, became effective for any application postmarked on or after October 1, 2023. This exemption now applies to all I-539 applicants, including categories like H-4, L-2, and E derivatives who were previously covered by a temporary suspension. While most applicants will no longer be scheduled for a biometrics appointment, USCIS retains the discretion to require biometrics on a case-by-case basis, in which instance an applicant will receive an appointment notice. USCIS also clarified that if an applicant mistakenly combines the biometric fee with the paper-based filing fee, the entire application will be rejected; however, if paid separately, only the biometric fee will be returned. <6> In response to pressure from officials in cities like New York, the Biden-Harris Administration announced new actions on September 20, 2023, to accelerate work permit processing for eligible migrants. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) initiated a campaign to raise awareness, sending over 1.4 million email and text notifications in English, Spanish, Haitian Creole, Ukrainian, and Russian to parolees, informing them of their eligibility to apply for employment authorization. As part of this effort, DHS also deployed 50 personnel to New York in September 2023 to help educate recently arrived migrants on the immigration system and the application process for work permits. These actions were part of a broader strategy that also included extending and redesignating Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for approximately 472,000 Venezuelan nationals who were already in the U.S. by July 31, 2023, making them newly eligible to apply for work authorization. <7> On September 13, 2023, Judge Andrew Hanen of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas declared the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) Final Rule to be unlawful. This ruling expanded on a previous decision from July 16, 2021, in which Judge Hanen first found the program illegal. The court determined that the Biden administration's 2022 attempt to codify DACA into a federal regulation had no substantive differences from the original 2012 memorandum and therefore suffered from the same legal issues. However, Judge Hanen maintained a partial stay of the injunction for individuals who received their initial DACA status on or before July 16, 2021. This allows current DACA recipients to retain their protection from deportation, renew their status, and keep their work authorizations while litigation continues. The ruling prevents the government from approving any new, first-time DACA applications. <8> In early September 2023, news outlets reported that the number of migrant families crossing the U.S.-Mexico border reached a record high in August 2023. [6, 13] The U.S. Border Patrol apprehended at least 91,000 migrants who crossed as part of a family group, surpassing the previous single-month record of 84,486 set in May 2019. [6] For the first time during the Biden administration, families became the largest demographic group crossing the border, surpassing single adults. [6] Overall, the Border Patrol conducted over 181,000 encounters between ports of entry along the Southwest border in August. [1] This influx created significant challenges, particularly in Arizona, where smugglers began directing migrants from countries as distant as Senegal, India, and China through perilous, remote desert regions like the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, despite extreme heat. [4] The Tucson Sector became the busiest along the border in July for the first time since 2008, with officials noting the presence of migrants from across the globe and calling the situation 'a real emergency'. [4] The U.S. Border Patrol conducted 3,212 rescues in August alone. [1] <9> On August 17, 2023, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reopened its international field office in Havana, Cuba. This initiative is part of the Biden-Harris Administration's broader strategy to restore the international presence of USCIS and to facilitate safe, legal, and orderly migration. The Havana office will provide services by appointment only, focusing on conducting interviews and processing pending cases for the Cuban Family Reunification Parole (CFRP) program and Form I-730, Refugee/Asylee Relative Petitions. It will also offer other limited services, such as refugee processing and collecting biometrics for U visa applications. The previous USCIS office in Havana was closed on December 10, 2018.

[2, 6, 7] The proposed legislation included funding for border security, aid for Ukraine and Israel, and provisions to grant the government emergency powers to manage the border. Campbell Barker of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas issued a 14-day administrative stay, temporarily halting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from approving applications under the program. [2] Specifically, there was a 32% decrease in such encounters compared to the previous month, June 2024. [2] This significant decline was attributed to a presidential proclamation and an interim final rule that were implemented on June 4, 2024, to temporarily suspend the entry of certain noncitizens. [2]

[1, 2, 3] The form has been renamed to "Application for Travel Documents, Parole Documents, and Arrival/Departure Records." [1, 2, 4, 9] This action builds upon Executive Order 14161, which was issued on January 20, 2025. [2, 4, 7] The restrictions, which direct government departments to implement stricter vetting processes, became effective at 12:01 a.m. EDT on June 9, 2025. [3, 5, 6, 7] The proclamation includes exceptions for lawful permanent residents, holders of valid visas issued before the effective date, dual nationals traveling on a passport from an unrestricted country, and other specific categories. [3, 6, 7] <5> On May 7, 2025, a bipartisan group of U.S. Representatives reintroduced the Farm Workforce Modernization Act of 2025, designated as H.R. 3227. The bill, led by Representatives Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) and Dan Newhouse (R-WA) along with others, aims to reform the nation's agricultural labor system to create a stable and reliable workforce for farmers and ranchers. Key provisions of the legislation include establishing a program for undocumented farmworkers to earn legal status through continued agricultural employment, reforming the H-2A guest worker program to provide more flexibility and accommodate year-round labor needs, and mandating a nationwide electronic employment verification system (similar to E-Verify) for all agricultural employers. This "self-deportation" program is managed through a repurposed government smartphone app called CBP Home, previously known as CBP One under the Biden administration. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), led by Secretary Kristi Noem, presented the initiative as a more cost-effective and dignified way for individuals to leave the U.S. compared to formal deportation, which costs an estimated $17,000 per person. The stipend is to be paid after the individual's departure is confirmed. Those who register for the program are to be deprioritized for arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). President Trump officially launched the program, dubbed "Project Homecoming," via an executive order announced on May 10, 2025. He stated that those who leave voluntarily might have a chance to return legally in the future if they are deemed "good," though no specific legal pathway for this was defined. <7> On May 5, 2025, Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and a group of 11 co-sponsors introduced the 'Immigration Parole Reform Act of 2025' in the U.S. Senate. [2, 3] This policy revives a rarely enforced 1996 law, which was previously used during the Trump administration in 2018. [1, 3, 6] Officials stated that the fines could be applied retroactively for up to five years and that the government might also seize property from those who do not pay. [1, 2, 3] The announcement is part of a broader series of measures aimed at encouraging self-deportation. [2, 3, 4] Documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request by the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) confirmed the directive was issued via an internal email on March 21, 2025, and was intended to last for approximately two weeks. [1] The news was first publicly reported on March 25, 2025. [1, 2, 3, 4] The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) stated the pause was necessary to implement enhanced screening and vetting procedures to identify potential fraud, public safety, or national security concerns. [2, 3, 5] This action was taken to align with two of President Trump's executive orders issued on January 20, 2025: EO 14161, "Protecting the United States from Foreign Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats," and EO 14157, "Designating Cartels and Other Organizations as Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists." [1, 2, 7, 6] An email on April 10, 2025, announced the lifting of the pause but advised that further guidance on interviews would be forthcoming. [1]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On July 23, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled 2-1 that an executive order by President Donald Trump intended to end birthright citizenship is unconstitutional. The court's opinion stated that the order is "invalid because it contradicts the plain language of the Fourteenth Amendment’s grant of citizenship to ‘all persons born in the United States and subject to the jurisdiction thereof.'" This ruling affirmed a lower-court's decision to issue a nationwide injunction, blocking the Trump administration from implementing the measure which sought to deny automatic citizenship to the U.S.-born children of undocumented immigrants or temporary foreign visitors. The White House, through spokeswoman Abigail Jackson, stated its disagreement with the ruling, asserting the court "misinterpreted the purpose and the text of the 14th Amendment," and announced its intention to appeal. The ruling was one of several legal challenges against the executive order, and it is anticipated that the issue will ultimately be decided by the Supreme Court. <2> On July 23, 2025, the American Immigration Council published a special report titled "Mass Deportation: Analyzing the Trump Administration's Attacks on Immigrants, Democracy, and America." The report provides a sweeping analysis of the first six months of a hypothetical second Trump administration, which began in January 2025. It asserts that this period has seen the most extreme immigration crackdown in modern U.S. history, which constitutes an attack on American democracy itself. Key findings highlighted in the report include the effective end of asylum at the southern border, the dismantling of the refugee program, and the weaponization of government power against immigrants. The authors state the administration's actions are "corrosive to the rule of law" and represent a "wholesale effort to use immigrants and the U.S. immigration system to attack core tenets of our democracy." The analysis also notes a clear division in how state and local governments have responded, with some pushing back to protect immigrant communities while others have advanced more punitive measures. <3> U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has announced new fees for various immigration forms and benefits. This change is mandated by the recently passed H.R. 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which was signed into law on July 4, 2025. The new fees are effective for all relevant applications and benefit requests that are postmarked on or after July 22, 2025. <4> On July 15, 2025, Representatives Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Florida) and Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) introduced the bipartisan Dignity Act of 2025 (H.R. 4393) in the U.S. House of Representatives. The bill, which is a revised version of a 2023 proposal, aims to reform the U.S. immigration system by enhancing border security, updating the asylum process, and creating a "Dignity Program." This seven-year program would offer a pathway to legal status for eligible undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. since the end of 2020, allowing them to work and travel legally provided they pass background checks and pay restitution. Additionally, the legislation seeks to address legal immigration backlogs by raising per-country visa caps from 7% to 15% and allowing applicants who have been waiting for more than ten years to pay a premium fee to expedite their visa. The bill also includes provisions to protect 'Documented Dreamers' from aging out of their legal status. <5> On July 10, 2025, U.S. District Judge Joseph N. Laplante of New Hampshire provisionally certified a nationwide class in the lawsuit *Barbara et al. v. Trump et al.*, which challenges President Trump's executive order aimed at ending birthright citizenship. [7] In the same order, Judge Laplante, a George W. Bush appointee, issued a nationwide preliminary injunction blocking the enforcement of the executive order. [2, 4, 7] This decision came in response to a new class-action lawsuit filed by the ACLU and other immigrant rights advocates following a June 27, 2025, Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of broad nationwide injunctions but suggested class actions could be an appropriate path for such relief. [4, 6, 7] The certified class includes all children born in the United States on or after February 20, 2025, to parents who are undocumented or in the country on temporary visas. [2, 4] Judge Laplante stayed his ruling for seven days to allow the Trump administration to file an appeal. [2, 7] <6> Multiple federal district courts have temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's executive order that sought to end birthright citizenship. Following legal challenges from a coalition of Democratic-led states and immigrant rights groups, several judges issued injunctions. On July 10, 2025, a federal court in New Hampshire blocked the order and certified a nationwide class-action lawsuit to protect all impacted children born in the U.S. This followed a Supreme Court decision in late June that limited the scope of nationwide injunctions, prompting groups like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and its partners to file a new class-action suit to ensure broad protection. Other judges, including Senior U.S. District Judge John Coughenour in Washington and U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, also issued separate rulings blocking the order, calling it "blatantly unconstitutional." The legal challenges were brought by states including Washington, Arizona, Illinois, and Oregon, alongside organizations such as the ACLU, the Legal Defense Fund, and CASA, who argued the executive order violates the 14th Amendment. <7> On July 10, 2025, a clash occurred between protesters and U.S. federal agents who were conducting an immigration raid on a farm in Southern California. [1] This confrontation was part of a broader increase in arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the region, with agents targeting various locations such as car washes and farms, which stoked widespread fear within immigrant communities. [1] <8> On July 1, 2025, the Senate passed its version of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” with a narrow 51-50 vote. The bill, which allocates significant funding for immigration enforcement, was then sent to the House of Representatives for final consideration before a presidential deadline of July 4. The legislation prioritizes major funding increases for immigration enforcement, including $45 billion for detention facilities and over $46 billion for border wall construction.

United States, the federal government has indicated its plan to resume processing initial applications for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program for individuals residing outside of Texas. The court's decision narrowed a previous nationwide injunction, limiting its effect to only Texas. Specifically, the ruling affirmed that deferred action (protection from deportation) is a lawful exercise of prosecutorial discretion nationwide, while finding the work permit component potentially unlawful only within Texas. Consequently, the government's proposal, which is still subject to approval by the district court under Judge Andrew Hanen, would allow new applicants outside of Texas to receive both protection from deportation and work permits for the first time since an injunction halted processing in 2021. As of May 2025, the ruling stood, as no party had appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. <3> On October 1, 2025, the U.S. federal government initiated a shutdown after Congress failed to pass the necessary funding legislation. Despite the shutdown, operations for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) continued. These agencies, along with most of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), are considered "essential" and therefore remained operational. While ICE's enforcement and removal activities proceeded, and CBP kept ports of entry open, some employees of these agencies worked without pay. Other immigration-related functions were affected; for example, the E-Verify system was taken offline, and the Department of Labor (DOL) suspended all its immigration-related activities as it is not fee-funded. <4> The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has issued a final rule, set to take effect on October 2, 2025, aimed at modernizing and streamlining the petitioning process for the H-2A temporary agricultural worker program. This initiative is designed to assist American farmers in more efficiently addressing labor shortages by allowing for the earlier electronic filing of petitions. Under the new rule, U.S. employers can electronically submit the new Form I-129H2A for unnamed agricultural workers after the Department of Labor (DOL) has accepted the application for a temporary labor certification (TLC), but before the TLC is officially approved. This procedural change permits U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to begin processing these petitions sooner, although final approval will still be contingent upon the DOL's approval of the TLC. The streamlined process initially applies to electronically filed petitions for unnamed beneficiaries; a future expansion is planned to include named beneficiaries. Paper-based applications will continue to use the existing Form I-129 and will not benefit from this early filing option. <5> U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), in collaboration with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), announced the results of 'Operation Twin Shield' on September 30, 2025. The operation, described as the first of its kind in terms of scale in a single geographic area, focused on over 1,000 cases with indicators of fraud or ineligibility. Officers conducted over 900 site visits and in-person interviews, which resulted in the discovery of suspected fraud in 275 cases. John Sauer asked the justices to review rulings from lower courts which had previously blocked the policy through nationwide injunctions. This legal challenge is part of a broader effort by the administration to address what it describes as a policy of 'prime importance' for border security. Opponents, including the ACLU, argue the executive order is illegal and unconstitutional. A previous Supreme Court decision in June had limited the scope of nationwide injunctions but did not rule on the core constitutionality of the birthright citizenship order itself. <7> On September 23, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that 2 million unauthorized immigrants had been removed or had voluntarily departed the United States since January 20, 2025. samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On December 12, 2025, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) issued updated operational guidance regarding the submission of photographs for immigration benefit requests. Under the new policy, USCIS will no longer accept self-submitted photos. Instead, all photographs must be taken directly by USCIS or an authorized entity, such as at an Application Support Center (ASC) during a Biometrics Services Appointment (BSA). Furthermore, the updated rules mandate that any reused photos must be no more than three years (36 months) old at the time of filing. <2> On December 5, 2025, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) announced the creation of a new, centralized vetting center. Headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, the center is designed to enhance the screening of immigration applications by utilizing advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, alongside intelligence and law enforcement partnerships. The initiative aims to identify and screen out individuals who pose a threat to national security and public safety, such as terrorists, individuals with criminal backgrounds, and those committing fraud, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. <3> U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has updated its Policy Manual to reduce the maximum validity period for certain Employment Authorization Documents (EADs). Effective December 5, 2025, the maximum validity period for initial and renewal EADs in several categories has been shortened from five years back to 18 months. The affected categories include individuals admitted as refugees, those granted asylum or withholding of removal, and applicants with pending applications for asylum, adjustment of status (under INA 245), or suspension of deportation/cancellation of removal (including NACARA relief). <4> On December 3, 2025, the U.S. Department of State announced a significant expansion of its visa screening and vetting procedures. Effective December 15, 2025, the agency is expanding its online presence review requirement to include all H-1B specialty occupation visa applicants and their H-4 dependents. To facilitate this digital vetting process, affected applicants are instructed to adjust the privacy settings on all of their social media profiles to 'public'. <5> On November 28, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a notice in the Federal Register (90 FR 54733) officially announcing the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti, effective February 3, 2026. <6> The U.S. Department of State officially paused all non-immigrant and immigrant visa issuances for Afghan nationals applying with an Afghan passport. The action effectively froze the Special Immigrant Visa (SIV) pipeline and all other visa categories for these individuals. The administration stated the pause was implemented to undergo a full review of security vetting and screening protocols due to grave national-security deficiencies in Afghan identity-management systems. Dual nationals applying with a valid passport from an exempt country were not subject to this pause. <7> A memorandum issued by the Director of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) ordered the review and rescreening of approximately 200,000 refugees admitted during the previous administration. Ur Jaddou serves as the USCIS Director as of early 2024. The topic relates to discussions of immigration policy under a second Trump administration. <8> On November 19, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to broadly expand the 'public charge' rule. The proposed rule would allow immigration officials to consider an applicant's past or future use of non-cash, means-tested public benefits—such as SNAP (nutritional benefits) and housing assistance—when evaluating applications for admission or lawful permanent residency (green cards). By rescinding the Biden administration's guardrails, the proposed changes signal a return to broader considerations of public benefit use, giving USCIS officers greater discretion to determine if an individual is likely to become a public charge. <9> The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) implemented a new $1,000 Immigration Parole Fee; This fee is effective October 16, 2025; This fee applies to individuals granted various forms of parole
